nodes.name: Co3O4 Hydrothermal Synthesis
nodes.procedure: 0.582 g of Co(NO3)2·6H2O, 0.6 g of CO(NH2)2, and 0.186 g of NH4F were dissolved in 40 mL of deionized water. The above solution and a piece of cleaned carbon cloth (C⊙, 2×3 cm²) were transferred to a 50 mL Teflon-lined stainless-steel autoclave. The autoclave was sealed and placed in an oven at 120 °C for 6 h and then cooled naturally. The resulting precursor supported on CC was washed repeatedly and then dried at 60 °C. After annealing at 350 °C for 2 h under air atmosphere, Co3O4 nanorod arrays were obtained.

nodes.name: Ru Loading on Co3O4
nodes.procedure: Ru/Co3O4 was prepared by placing the Co3O4 in 50 mL of ethanol solution. After vigorous ultrasonic treatment for 30 min, 500 μL of ruthenium chloride aqueous solution (20 mg mL^-1) was slowly dropped into ethanol solution and then dried at 80 °C. Subsequently, the dried Co3O4 was placed in a muffle furnace and annealed at 250 °C for 2 h under air atmosphere. The samples were washed four times with H2O, and dried in a vacuum overnight.

nodes.name: CVD Phosphorization for Ru/Co3O4-CoP and Co3O4-CoP
nodes.procedure: Ru/Co3O4 CoP was prepared by a chemical vapor deposition (CVD) approach, where the 300 mg of NaH2PO2 was placed in the upstream, and the Ru/Co3O4 was placed in the downstream. The CVD process was carried out for 2 h under argon atmosphere (50 mL min^-1) at 350 °C. For comparison, the pristine Co3O4 was treated with the same CVD process as that for Ru/Co3O4-CoP to prepare Co3O4-CoP.

nodes.name: Electrochemical Activation
nodes.procedure: Co(OH)2 CoP, Ru/Co(OH)2 and Ru/Co(OH)2-CoP were prepared by electrochemical activation of Co3O4 CoP, Ru/Co3O4 and Ru/Co3O4 CoP using an electrochemical workstation (CHI 760e, Chenhua Instrument Co., LTD) in an H-type cell separated by a Nafion 211 membrane. The self-supported catalysts, a Pt foil and a saturated calomel electrode (SCE) were used as the cathode, the counter and the reference electrodes, respectively. The catalysts were electrochemical activated in 0.5 M KOH + 20 mM KNO3 aqueous solution at -0.2 V for 1 h. Then, the samples were washed with water and acetone, and dried under Ar atmosphere.

nodes.characterization_summary: Typical diffraction peaks at 19.1°, 32.6°, 38.0° and 51.5° attributed to (001), (100), (011) and (012) planes of Co(OH)₂ phase. No distinct CoP peaks observed, suggesting amorphous CoP state.
nodes.evidence_snippet: X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns (Fig. 2a) show that the typical diffraction peaks at 19.1°, 32.6°, 38.0° and 51.5° are attributed to the (001), (100), (011) and (012) planes of Co(OH)₂ (PDF # 74-1057), indicating the formation of Co(OH)₂ phase in Ru/Co(OH)₂ and Ru/Co(OH)₂–CoP. The absence of distinct characteristic peaks of CoP (PDF # 89-2747) suggests that the CoP may exist in an amorphous state.

nodes.characterization_summary: SEM images show catalysts retain nanorod morphology throughout synthetic process and formation of Co(OH)₂ nanosheets after electrochemical activation.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images (Figs. S2–S4) show that the catalysts retain the nanorod morphology throughout the synthetic process ... leading to the formation of Co(OH)₂ nanosheets (Figs. 2b and S8).

nodes.characterization_summary: HRTEM shows no lattice fringes in core of nanorods indicating amorphous CoP maintained, 0.24 nm interplanar spacing at edges attributed to Co(OH)₂ (011) plane.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) image and high resolution TEM (HRTEM) image of Ru/Co(OH)₂–CoP (Figs. 2c and S9-S11) show that no lattice is observed in the core of the nanorods, indicating that the amorphous structure of CoP is maintained. At the edges of the nanorods, a interplanar spacing of 0.24 nm is attributed to Co(OH)₂ (011) plane.

nodes.characterization_summary: Aberration-corrected HAADF-STEM confirms highly dispersed Ru nanoclusters with average particle size 1.25 nm on Co(OH)₂–CoP nanosheets.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Aberration-corrected high-angle annular darkfield scanning electron microscopy (HAADF-STEM) image of the nanosheets further confirms the formation of highly dispersed Ru nanoclusters with an average particle size of 1.25 nm (Fig. 2e and Fig. S14).

nodes.characterization_summary: Ru K-edge XANES shows K-edge position between Ru foil and RuO₂, indicating oxidation state of Ru species between 0 and +4.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The Ru K-edge XANES (Fig. 2g) shows that the K-edge position of the Ru in Ru/Co(OH)₂–CoP is between those of Ru foil and RuO₂, indicating an oxidation state of Ru species between 0 and +4.

nodes.characterization_summary: Fourier transform EXAFS shows Ru–Ru at 2.36 Å and Ru–O at 1.53 Å. EXAFS fitting gives coordination numbers Ru–O: 5.35, Ru–P: 0.66, Ru–Ru: 1.59, confirming Ru nanocluster formation.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Fourier transform of the EXAFS spectra without phase correction (Fig. 2h) displays distinct scattering peaks at 2.36 Å and 1.53 Å, which are attributed to the Ru–Ru and Ru–O coordination of Ru/Co(OH)₂–CoP ... coordination numbers of Ru–O, Ru–P and Ru–Ru obtained by fitting the EXAFS spectra are 5.35, 0.66 and 1.59 (Fig. 2i and Table S1).

nodes.characterization_summary: Co 2p, P 2p, Ru 3p and O 1s XPS spectra show formation of CoP, Co(OH)₂ and metallic Ru phases.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Co 2p, P 2p, Ru 3p and O 1s XPS spectra of Ru/Co(OH)₂ CoP show the formation of CoP, Co(OH)₂ and metallic Ru phases (Figs. S15–S20).

nodes.characterization_summary: UPS shows work function of CoP 5.95 eV, Co(OH)₂ 5.78 eV, Co(OH)₂-CoP heterojunction 5.86 eV, and Ru 5.65 eV, indicating heterostructure formation and electron transfer.
nodes.evidence_snippet: CoP exhibits a work function of 5.95 eV, significantly higher than that of Co(OH)₂ (5.78 eV). Upon the formation of a junction ... Ru showing a lower work function of 5.65 eV compared to that of Co(OH)₂–CoP (5.86 eV).

nodes.characterization_summary: EIS shows Ru/Co(OH)₂–CoP has lowest charge transfer resistance Rct of 2.03 Ω.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Ru/Co(OH)₂ CoP displays the lowest Rct of 2.03 Ω, unveiling that it possesses more efficient NO₃⁻RR kinetics (Table S6).

nodes.characterization_summary: Double-layer capacitance Cdl from CV: Ru/Co(OH)₂–CoP 37.09 mF cm⁻¹, Ru/Co(OH)₂ 18.31 mF cm⁻¹, Co(OH)₂–CoP 5.75 mF cm⁻¹, indicating highest ECSA for Ru/Co(OH)₂–CoP.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The electrochemically active surface areas (Fig. S40) were estimated based on double-layer capacitance (Cdl), with Ru/Co(OH)₂–CoP displaying the highest Cdl value of 37.09 mF cm⁻¹ (Co(OH)₂ CoP: 5.75 mF cm⁻¹; Ru/Co(OH)₂: 18.31 mF cm⁻¹), which suggests a exposure of more active sites.

nodes.characterization_summary: In situ Raman confirms transformation of Co₃O₄ to Co(OH)₂ during electrochemical activation.
nodes.evidence_snippet: In situ Raman spectroscopy of Ru/Co₃O₄–CoP again confirms the transformation of Co₃O₄ to Co(OH)₂ (Fig. S13).
